Find, from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament, and the Jewish and Christian literature around them (Targum,
Mishnah, Talmud, midrash, pseudepigrapha, Christian apocrypha, Church Fathers, Syriac homilies), every text an
advanced reader of this commentary should have beside it. Judge each text on what it says in its own place, not
on resemblance of a word. Weigh at least:

- paralel: the same figure, scene or story told in the other scripture;
- motif: a shared image, formula, liturgical act or ethical motif without a shared story;
- karsi_anlati: the Qur'an tells it differently, corrects or answers it; the difference is the point;
- soydas: a Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac cognate of a key word of these ayat and how the other scripture uses it;
- yorum_gelenegi: Jewish or Christian interpretation of a parallel text that changes what the parallel means.

Before grading, work through every distinct scene, object, action, relation, formula and secondary sense
actually developed in the commentary, including any v16 augment additions. Recall direct formulations, repeated
occurrences, nonlexical parallels, relevant reversals and interpretive traditions. Do not let the title, first
scene or already quoted passages stand in for the whole page. For a Buluşmalar section, consider the particular
meetings between images its prose develops. Root/branch labels are not dictionary definitions, evidence of
cognacy or permission to import an undeveloped sense. Do this review internally; output only candidate rows.

Use the package's Semitic root table: for every Arabic root it lists, recall how the corresponding Hebrew or
Aramaic root is used across the Hebrew Bible, passages that play on the same consonants, and passages whose
wording shows a difference from what the ayah says. Propose such passages as soydas (shared root), motif,
paralel or karsi_anlati as fits, and name the basis in `basis` (the root, and whether it is the table's sound
correspondence or your own recollection). Same consonants with an unrelated sense are not a connection.

Every explanation must identify a particular detail or claim in the commentary, the corresponding detail in
the candidate's own context, and what the relationship adds. Shared vocabulary, a broad religious theme or
the same speaker alone is insufficient. Do not invent imagery that neither text supports. A shared word is
not required. Preserve indirect, secondary and contrary readings with a concrete connection; do not choose
one preferred reading. A parallel is not a dependence: say what the texts share, not who borrowed.

Check the speaker, addressee, action, negation and verse boundary in remembered context. Name a neighbouring
verse separately when its own contribution is necessary; proximity alone does not qualify it. Keep Hebrew,
Aramaic, Syriac and Greek quotations short and specific to the cited passage and witness. If exact wording or
numbering is uncertain, explain the connection and uncertainty in English instead of reconstructing a quote.
Label roots, dictionary forms and wording from the source commentary explicitly. Never combine verses into

Include every candidate meeting this standard. There is no target list length. Strong means a direct,
specific correspondence, including a secondary feature developed in the prose. Medium means a specific
correspondence with an explicit interpretive bridge. Weak means a plausible, specific connection whose
uncertainty you identify; it still cannot be generic. Counter-narrative is a relationship kind, not weaker
confidence. Model agreement and a follow-up origin never make a claim verified.

strength	tradition	kind	ref	basis	short_explanation

## Frozen commentary (Turkish)

Bu surenin kelimeleri ayetteki anlamlarıyla okunur; aşağıdaki imgeler o anlamın yanında duyulur, onun yerine geçmez. İlk sahne pazardır. Tüccar malını ortaya koyar; alışveriş ya kâr getirir ya ana paradan yer. Kayıp kelimesinin dalı tam bu işleyişi adlandırır: {ar:خسر التاجر إذا وضع من رأس ماله, tr:hasira't-tâcir izâ vada'a min re'si mâlih, gloss:tüccar sermayesinden eksildiğinde "hasira" denir, source:"خ س ر,B002"}, {ar:صفقة خاسرة أي غير مربحة, tr:safka hâsira, gloss:kâr getirmeyen alışveriş, source:"خ س ر,B002"}. Aynı ailenin bir başka dalı teraziye geçer: {ar:كلته ووزنته فأخسرته أي نقصته, tr:kiltuhû ve vezentuhû fe-ahsertuhû, gloss:ölçüp tarttım da eksik verdim, source:"خ س ر,B003"}. Kayıp burada bir duygu değil, bir hesaptır: ana para azalır, kefe hafif kalır.

Birinci ayetin kelimesi {ar:وَٱلْعَصْرِ, tr:ve'l-asr, gloss:asra andolsun, source:103:1} en geniş anlamıyla uzun bir zamandır: {ar:العصر الدهر, tr:el-asru'd-dehr, gloss:asr, uzun zaman, source:"ع ص ر,B001"}. Ardından gelen ikinci ayet insanı kaybın "içine" yerleştirir: {ar:إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ, tr:inne'l-insâne le-fî husr, gloss:insan gerçekten kayıp içindedir, source:103:2}. İki ayet yan yana durunca harcanan sermayenin zamanın kendisi olduğu görünür: alışveriş açık kaldıkça sermaye erir. Düz bir "insan ziyandadır" cümlesi kaybın tek seferlik bir olay olmadığını, işleyen bir eksilme olduğunu göstermez. Kur'an sermayenin neye kadar indiğini de söyler; Peygamber'e söylemesi emredilen sözde kaybedilen şey insanın kendisidir: {ar:إِنَّ ٱلْخَٰسِرِينَ ٱلَّذِينَ خَسِرُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُمْ وَأَهْلِيهِمْ, tr:inne'l-hâsirîne'llezîne hasirû enfusehum ve ehlîhim, gloss:asıl kaybedenler kendilerini ve ailelerini kaybedenlerdir, source:39:15}. Elde olanın bitip gittiği de açıkça konur: {ar:مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ ۖ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍۢ, tr:mâ indekum yenfed ve mâ indallâhi bâk, gloss:sizdeki tükenir, Allah katındaki kalır, source:16:96}. Hemen sonraki surede mal biriktirip sayan kişi sermayesini zamandan uzun yaşayacak bir şey sanır: {ar:يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُۥ, tr:yahsebu enne mâlehû ahledeh, gloss:malının kendisini ölümsüz kıldığını sanır, source:104:3}.

Kötü alışverişin Kur'an'daki sahnesi, hidayeti verip sapıklığı satın alanlardır; Allah onlar için hesabı kapatır: {ar:فَمَا رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمْ, tr:fe-mâ rabihat ticâratuhum, gloss:ticaretleri kâr getirmedi, source:2:16}. Terazide eksiltme de aynı kökle söylenir; ölçerken eksik verenler {ar:يُخْسِرُونَ, tr:yuhsirûn, gloss:eksiltirler, source:83:3}, gökle birlikte kurulan dengeyle ilgili buyruk {ar:وَلَا تُخْسِرُوا۟ ٱلْمِيزَانَ, tr:ve lâ tuhsiru'l-mîzân, gloss:teraziyi eksik tutmayın, source:55:9}, Şuayb'ın kavmine sözü {ar:أَوْفُوا۟ ٱلْكَيْلَ وَلَا تَكُونُوا۟ مِنَ ٱلْمُخْسِرِينَ, tr:evfu'l-keyle ve lâ tekûnû mine'l-muhsirîn, gloss:ölçüyü tam verin, eksik verenlerden olmayın, source:26:181}. Ölçüyü tam vermeyi de içeren buyruk listesi şu sözle kapanır: {ar:ذَٰلِكُمْ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ, tr:zâlikum vassâkum bih, gloss:size bunu tavsiye etti, source:6:152}; tam ölçü ile tavsiye aynı ayette buluşur.

Üçüncü ayetin istisnası başka bir alışverişten yapılır. Kur'an iman edenlere böyle bir ticareti kendisi gösterir: {ar:هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَىٰ تِجَٰرَةٍۢ تُنجِيكُم مِّنْ عَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍۢ, tr:hel edullukum alâ ticâratin tuncîkum, gloss:sizi acı azaptan kurtaracak bir ticarete yol göstereyim mi, source:61:10} ve malın adı hemen konur: {ar:تُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ, tr:tu'minûne billâhi ve rasûlih, gloss:Allah'a ve elçisine inanırsınız, source:61:11}. Okuyan, namaz kılan, gizli açık harcayanlar {ar:يَرْجُونَ تِجَٰرَةًۭ لَّن تَبُورَ, tr:yercûne ticâraten len tebûr, gloss:asla batmayacak bir ticaret umarlar, source:35:29}. Bir yerde alıcı Allah'tır: {ar:إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱشْتَرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمْ, tr:innallâhe'şterâ mine'l-mu'minîne enfusehum, gloss:Allah müminlerden canlarını satın aldı, source:9:111}; aynı ayette vaat {ar:وَعْدًا عَلَيْهِ حَقًّۭا, tr:va'den aleyhi hakkâ, gloss:üzerine borç bir vaat, source:9:111} diye bağlanır. Üçüncü ayetin kelimeleri bu pazarda birer karşılık bulur: {ar:عاملت الرجل أعامله معاملة في المبايعة وغيرها, tr:âmeltu'r-racule muâmeleten fi'l-mubâya'a, gloss:alışverişte biriyle muamele ettim, source:"ع م ل,B005"}; güvenin karşılığı {ar:الأمانة ضد الخيانة, tr:el-emânetu ziddu'l-hiyâne, gloss:emanet hıyanetin zıddıdır, source:"ء م ن,B001"}; hak da kişiye düşen paydır: {ar:الحق واحد الحقوق, tr:el-hakku vâhidu'l-hukûk, gloss:hak, haklardan biri, kişinin payı, source:"ح ق ق,B003"}. Kur'an borç ayetinde borçluyu tam bu kelimeyle anar: {ar:وَلْيُمْلِلِ ٱلَّذِى عَلَيْهِ ٱلْحَقُّ, tr:velyumlili'llezî aleyhi'l-hakk, gloss:hak üzerinde olan (borçlu) yazdırsın, source:2:282}. Birbirine hakkı tavsiye etmek, bu sahnede herkesin ötekine borçlu olduğunu teslim etmesidir. Sabır kelimesinin bir dalı da tartısız alışverişi anlatır: {ar:اشتريت الشيء صبرة أي بلا وزن ولا كيل, tr:iştereytu'ş-şey'e subraten, gloss:şeyi yığın hâlinde, tartmadan ölçmeden aldım, source:"ص ب ر,B011"}. Kayıp eksik tartıyla başlamıştı; sabrın karşılığı ise tartıya hiç girmez: {ar:إِنَّمَا يُوَفَّى ٱلصَّٰبِرُونَ أَجْرَهُم بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍۢ, tr:innemâ yuveffe's-sâbirûne ecrahum bi-gayri hisâb, gloss:sabredenlere ücretleri hesapsız tam ödenir, source:39:10}.

Aynı sahnenin öteki yüzü gündelikçidir. Asr, günün geç vaktidir: {ar:العصر العشي, tr:el-asru'l-aşiyy, gloss:asr, akşamüstü, source:"ع ص ر,B001"}; bu vakit adını bir namaza da verir {ar:صلاة العصر, tr:salâtu'l-asr, gloss:ikindi namazı, source:"ع ص ر,B001"}. Günün işi orada biter ve ücret vadesine gelir. Amel hem kasıtlı iştir {ar:كل فعل يكون من الحيوان بقصد, tr:kullu fi'lin yekûnu mine'l-hayevâni bi-kasd, gloss:canlıdan kasıtla çıkan her iş, source:"ع م ل,B001"}, hem eliyle kuyu kazıp ören ekip {ar:العملة القوم يعملون بأيديهم ضروبا من العمل حفرا أو طيا, tr:el-amele, gloss:elleriyle kazma, örme gibi işler yapan topluluk, source:"ع م ل,B006"}, hem de işin ücreti {ar:العمالة أجر ما عمل, tr:el-umâle ecru mâ amil, gloss:yapılan işin ücreti, source:"ع م ل,B004"}. Hakkın vadesi gelmiştir {ar:حق الشيء وجب, tr:hakka'ş-şey'u vecebe, gloss:şey gerekli, ödenmesi zorunlu oldu, source:"ح ق ق,B002"}; sabır kökünde ise borcun arkasında duran kefil vardır {ar:الصبير هو الكفيل, tr:es-sabîr huve'l-kefîl, gloss:sabîr, kefildir, source:"ص ب ر,B003"}. İşin "salih" oluşu da öncelikle işler için söylenir: {ar:الصلاح ضد الفساد مختصان في أكثر الاستعمال بالأفعال, tr:es-salâhu ziddu'l-fesâd, gloss:salâh bozukluğun zıddıdır, ikisi çoğunlukla işler için kullanılır, source:"ص ل ح,B001"}. Aynı istisnayı başka bir yemin suresi ücretin adını koyarak tekrarlar: {ar:إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ فَلَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍۢ, tr:illellezîne âmenû ve amilu's-sâlihâti fe-lehum ecrun gayru memnûn, gloss:iman edip salih işler yapanlar hariç; onlara kesintisiz bir ücret var, source:95:6}. Çalışanla ücretin adı ve sabır bir başka yerde aynı cümlede birleşir: {ar:نِعْمَ أَجْرُ ٱلْعَٰمِلِينَ, tr:ni'me ecru'l-âmilîn, gloss:çalışanların ücreti ne güzel, source:29:58}, {ar:ٱلَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا۟ وَعَلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ يَتَوَكَّلُونَ, tr:ellezîne saberû, gloss:sabredenler ve Rablerine dayananlar, source:29:59}. İnsanın elinde kalan, emeğinden başkası değildir: {ar:وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَٰنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ, tr:ve en leyse li'l-insâni illâ mâ seâ, gloss:insan için çalıştığından başkası yoktur, source:53:39}, ve ödeme günün sonundadır: {ar:وَإِنَّمَا تُوَفَّوْنَ أُجُورَكُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ, tr:ve innemâ tuveffevne ucûrakum yevme'l-kıyâme, gloss:ücretleriniz ancak kıyamet günü tam ödenir, source:3:185}. Bütün gün çalışıp eli boş kalanların adı da kayıp köküyle konur: {ar:بِٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ أَعْمَٰلًا, tr:bi'l-ahserîne a'mâlâ, gloss:işleri bakımından en çok kaybedenler, source:18:103}. Pazarın kapanacağı da söylenir: {ar:مِّن قَبْلِ أَن يَأْتِىَ يَوْمٌۭ لَّا بَيْعٌۭ فِيهِ وَلَا خُلَّةٌۭ, tr:min kabli en ye'tiye yevmun lâ bey'un fîh, gloss:içinde alışveriş ve dostluk olmayan gün gelmeden önce, source:2:254}; o anda insan kısa bir vade ister: {ar:رَبِّ لَوْلَآ أَخَّرْتَنِىٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍۢ قَرِيبٍۢ فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ, tr:rabbi levlâ ahhartenî ilâ ecelin karîb, gloss:Rabbim, beni yakın bir süreye ertelesen de sadaka verip salihlerden olsam, source:63:10}.

## Whole surah (Arabic)

103:1	وَٱلْعَصْرِ
103:2	إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ
103:3	إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَعَمِلُوا۟ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ

item.text: The briefs define several distinct threads: diminishing capital, false measures, mutual duties, day labor and wages, and limited time. I’m preserving those as separate TSV connections, with cognate claims marked as uncertain where the package’s root table does not verify them.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec1/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hos.12.9	merchant; deceitful scales	The commentary makes loss a market account and names underweighing; Hosea condemns a merchant who keeps deceitful scales and loves to oppress. It joins commercial fraud to character.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.5	false ephah and heavy shekel	The commentary's underweight scale has a close market scene here: sellers shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel, and wait for the Sabbath to end. Amos exposes fraud hidden behind ordinary trade.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.6	buying the poor for silver	The commentary treats a person's due share as a debt; Amos's merchants want to acquire the poor for silver and the needy for sandals. The passage shows false trade turning into human exploitation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.35	false measures and weights	The commentary describes a light scale pan and a diminished measure; Leviticus forbids falsifying measures of length, weight, or capacity. It makes fair exchange a covenantal duty.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.36	just balance, weights, and measures	Where the commentary contrasts a short measure with a full one, Leviticus specifies the correct balance and standard measures. The detail grounds just trade in a public rule.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.11.1	false balance	The commentary's underweight scale is condemned directly: Proverbs calls a false balance an abomination and contrasts it with a full weight. The text adds the moral status of the market device.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Mic.6.11	wicked scales and false weights	The commentary's seller who gives short measure is echoed by Micah's question about acquitting wicked scales and a bag of false weights. The prophet makes commercial fraud a test of justice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.25.15	full weight and long days	The commentary sets the loss of capital against time running out; Deuteronomy links a full, just weight with long life in the land. Honest trade sustains communal life across time.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.13	wages kept overnight	The commentary says a worker's wage has come due; Leviticus forbids keeping a hired worker's pay overnight. It gives the due wage a concrete deadline.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.14	oppressing the poor hired worker	The commentary treats work as labor that earns a right; Deuteronomy forbids oppressing a needy hired worker, whether Israelite or resident foreigner. It extends wage justice beyond one's own kin.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.15	pay before sunset	The commentary's day laborer reaches the wage deadline at day's end; Deuteronomy requires payment before sunset because the worker depends on it, and says the worker may cry to God. It makes delay a matter of life and justice.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.31.7	wages changed ten times	The commentary presents wage as a worker's due; Jacob tells his household that Laban deceived him and repeatedly changed his wages. The narrative gives a concrete case of an employer manipulating the account.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.22.13	neighbor's labor without pay	The commentary says the worker's wage is due; Jeremiah condemns a ruler who builds by making his neighbor work without pay. The unpaid labor is framed as injustice in the ruler's household and public power.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.7.2	laborer waiting for wages	The commentary pictures the day laborer reaching the end of work and awaiting pay; Job compares human life to a hired worker longing for shade and waiting for wages. The image makes mortality itself feel like exhausting labor.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Hag.1.6	wages in a purse with holes	The commentary describes principal steadily dwindling; Haggai pictures people earning wages only to put them into a pierced purse, alongside meager harvest and food. It turns economic loss into the felt result of wasted labor.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.2.22	gain from toil under the sun	The commentary makes time the capital spent in work; Ecclesiastes asks what a person gains from all toil and anxious effort under the sun. The question sharpens the uncertainty of labor's return.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Eccl.9.10	work before death	The commentary says the market will close and the worker's day will end; Ecclesiastes urges doing with might what one's hand finds, because there is no work in Sheol. It makes finite time the condition for action.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.55.2	spending and laboring without satisfaction	The commentary warns that capital can be spent without profit; Isaiah asks why people spend money on what is not bread and labor for what does not satisfy. The prophet turns failed exchange into a summons to seek what truly nourishes.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.13.11	wealth dwindling or gathering gradually	The commentary describes a trade that eats away at principal; Proverbs contrasts wealth that dwindles with wealth gathered little by little. It adds a scriptural contrast between erosion and patient accumulation.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.1	uncertain tomorrow	The commentary makes each passing moment part of the capital being spent; Proverbs warns against boasting about tomorrow because one does not know what a day will bring. It grounds the deadline in uncertainty.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Zech.8.16	speak truth to one's neighbor	The commentary says people counsel one another to the truth and to each person's right; Zechariah commands each person to speak truth to a neighbor and judge truthfully at the gates. It gives mutual truth-telling a civic setting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Lev.19.17	rebuke a neighbor	The commentary's reciprocal counsel implies speaking when another is wrong; Leviticus commands rebuking a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin. It makes moral correction part of mutual responsibility.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.24.19	gleanings left for the vulnerable	The commentary calls haqq a person's due share; Deuteronomy requires a forgotten sheaf to remain for the foreigner, orphan, and widow. It makes the vulnerable person's claim visible in ordinary harvest work.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.25.4	do not muzzle the threshing ox	The commentary includes work done by hands and the wage due for labor; Deuteronomy forbids muzzling an ox while it threshes. The law recognizes a worker's right to benefit while producing.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Eccl.2.22	Arabic root ع م ل; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew עמל	The commentary labels ʿamal as intentional work, manual labor, and its wage; Ecclesiastes uses עמל for toil and asks its gain. The shared labor term links work to uncertain return, though the table does not verify cognacy.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.15.6	Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ	The commentary labels belief with the root ء م ن; Genesis says Abram trusted God and it was counted as righteousness. The Hebrew usage adds trust in a promise to the commentary's faith-and-action condition; cognacy remains unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Hab.2.4	Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew אמנ	The commentary makes belief one condition for escaping loss; Habakkuk says the righteous live by faithfulness (emunah) amid arrogant violence. The Hebrew context adds steadfast fidelity to belief; the table's correspondence is unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.30.8	Arabic root ح ق ق; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חקק	The commentary glosses haqq as a person's share or right; Proverbs asks for the speaker's allotted portion of bread. Hebrew ḥōq as prescribed allotment offers a specific lexical bridge, but not proof of cognacy.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.41.49	Arabic root ص ب ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צבר	The commentary's Arabic lexical branch calls a ṣubrah a heap bought without weighing or measuring; Genesis says Joseph piled grain like the sand of the sea until he stopped counting it. The shared heap image is striking, though the Hebrew grain is stored, not sold.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Prov.13.25	Arabic root خ س ر; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew חסר	The commentary labels loss as principal diminished and a scale made deficient; Proverbs says the wicked person's belly lacks while the righteous eats to satisfaction. The Hebrew lack-word supplies a concrete deficit image, though cognacy is unverified.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Josh.1.8	Arabic root ص ل ح; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew צלח	The commentary labels ṣāliḥāt as righteous deeds; Joshua says keeping and doing the Torah leads to a way that prospers (צלח). The Hebrew use connects right action with success, while the root correspondence remains unverified and the meanings are not identical.
strong	tevrat	soydas	Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a	Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew/Aramaic אמנ	The commentary glosses amānah as trust opposed to betrayal; at judgment the Talmud asks whether a person conducted business faithfully. This joins trust to commerce in the same concrete setting, though cognacy is unverified.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Avot 2:15	short day, abundant work, great reward	The commentary's human life is capital spent in work and paid at day's end; Rabbi Tarfon says the day is short, the work abundant, and the reward great. The saying compresses the commentary's time-and-wage image into one maxim.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Avot 3:16	open shop, ledger, daily collectors	The commentary imagines time as capital and a final account; Avot depicts the world as an open shop with credit, a ledger, and collectors making daily rounds. It turns daily life into a debt that will be collected.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Avot 4:17	one hour for deeds in this world	The commentary insists that work must be done before the market closes; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world outweighs the whole life of the world to come. It makes present time the irreplaceable arena of action.
strong	tevrat	motif	Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 83a	porters' wages and confiscated cloaks	The commentary treats a laborer's wage as a right; in this story an employer takes porters' cloaks after they break barrels, and Rav orders him to return the cloaks and pay them. The case gives worker rights priority over the employer's loss.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 5:7	do not delay turning back	The commentary ends with a person asking for a little more time to give and do right; Sirach warns not to delay turning to the Lord, since judgment can come suddenly. It makes postponement itself a danger.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 11:19	wealth cannot secure one's remaining time	The commentary rejects the belief that amassed wealth can outlast time; Sirach describes a rich person who plans to enjoy his goods but does not know how soon he will die and leave them. It directly joins capital to a life one cannot extend.
strong	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 5:15	reward of the righteous	The commentary pictures righteous workers receiving their wage; Wisdom says the righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord. It gives the wage image an explicitly enduring outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Acts.3.1	ninth-hour prayer	The commentary names al-ʿaṣr as the afternoon prayer; Acts says Peter and John went to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. The shared practice is an afternoon prayer rhythm, not an identical named rite.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.9.4	work while it is day	The commentary sets the day worker's labor against the day's end; Jesus says his work must be done while it is day, since night is coming when no one can work. The saying makes the workday a figure for a closing opportunity.
strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Matt.20.8	workers paid at evening	The commentary's day laborer reaches the wage deadline at the day's end; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner orders the workers called and paid when evening comes. The scene directly joins a day's labor to its wage.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.10.7	laborer worthy of wages	The commentary treats wages as the worker's due; Jesus tells the traveling disciples that the laborer deserves his wages while they stay in a household. It applies the wage-right formula to religious workers.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.2	steward called to account	The commentary makes business an account whose capital can be lost; the rich man in Jesus' parable demands an account from a steward accused of squandering his property. It makes stewardship answerable before the owner.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.10	faithful or dishonest with little	The commentary glosses trust as the opposite of betrayal; Jesus says faithfulness in little predicts faithfulness in much, and dishonesty in little predicts dishonesty in much. The next verse applies this to money, making trust a test of stewardship.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.19	settling accounts after a long time	The commentary says capital is spent as time passes; in the talents parable the master returns after a long time and settles accounts with the servants entrusted with money. It links investment, delay, and reckoning.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.19.13	trade until the master's return	The commentary makes the market open only for a limited time; the nobleman tells servants to conduct business with the entrusted money until he returns. The parable makes the interval before return a period of accountable investment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.19.15	returns examined for gains	The commentary imagines an account closing after a period of work; on returning, the nobleman summons the servants to learn what each gained in trade. The scene makes the yield of entrusted capital reviewable.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.19	treasure consumed by moth and rust	The commentary warns that what one owns is used up; Jesus says earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth, rust, and thieves. It supplies a concrete image of stored capital that cannot be secured.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.6.20	treasure that does not decay	Against the commentary's eroding principal, Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy. It redirects investment toward a durable return.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.19	rich man expects many years of ease	The commentary rejects the idea that wealth makes a person outlive time; the rich fool tells his soul to rest because he has goods stored for many years. The speech exposes the assumed conversion of capital into extra life.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	soul required that night	The commentary says a market will close and a person may then ask for more time; God tells the rich fool his life is required that very night. It makes the deadline sudden and non-negotiable.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.4.13	merchants plan trade and profit	The commentary treats lifetime as capital spent in exchange; James addresses people planning to travel, trade, and make a profit for a year. The passage puts the trader's plan inside an uncertain lifespan.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.4.14	life as a passing mist	The commentary says the human being remains inside loss as time passes; James calls life a mist that appears briefly and vanishes. It gives the dwindling capital of time an explicit image.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.6.2	now is the day of salvation	The commentary warns that the final day has no market or chance to transact; Paul quotes Isaiah to say now is the acceptable time and now the day of salvation. It makes the present the open window for action.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.3.8	wage according to labor	The commentary links work to the wage due; Paul says the planter and waterer are one and each will receive a wage according to labor. It directly connects effort to compensation.
strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	SBLGNT:1Cor.9.10	Paul's reading of the unmuzzled ox	The commentary says the worker has a right to the wage of the work; Paul reads Deuteronomy's rule against muzzling a threshing ox as written for human workers, so the plowman and thresher may share in the crop. This Christian interpretation extends the law's protection to laborers.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.5.18	worker deserves wages	The commentary says the wage is owed when work is done; in instructions about elders, Paul cites the saying that the worker deserves his wages. It applies the laborer's due to support for community leaders.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.5.4	withheld harvest wages cry out	The commentary makes wage a due share; James says the wages withheld from field workers cry out and have reached the Lord of hosts. It links labor injustice to divine hearing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Jas.2.17	faith without works is dead	The commentary names belief and righteous deeds together; James says faith without works is dead. The passage makes action integral to a living faith, rather than a separate supplement.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.1.3	work of faith, labor of love, endurance of hope	The commentary's exception combines belief, righteous work, and patient endurance; Paul recalls the Thessalonians' work of faith, labor of love, and steadfastness of hope. The triad closely joins the same kinds of action.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.14	mutual correction and patience	The commentary says people urge one another toward what is right and toward patience; Paul tells the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all. It supplies concrete forms of reciprocal counsel.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	stir one another to love and good works	The commentary makes mutual urging toward truth and patience part of the exception; Hebrews tells hearers to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works. It gives mutual exhortation an explicitly ethical aim.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.25	encourage one another as the Day approaches	The commentary says the market closes on a coming day; Hebrews commands mutual encouragement all the more as the Day draws near. The approaching deadline intensifies communal action.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.36	endurance after doing God's will	The commentary joins patient endurance to a wage still to be received; Hebrews says endurance is needed after doing God's will to receive the promise. It makes waiting part of completed work.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	harvest in due season	The commentary's patient worker receives a wage after labor; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good, for a harvest will come in due season if one does not give up. It joins patient action to delayed return.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.8.14	abundance supplies another's need	The commentary calls haqq each person's share and mutual recognition of another's due; Paul says one community's abundance should supply another's need so there may be equality. It turns right share into reciprocal material care.
